title: US economy heats up on AI investment, consumer spending
summary: The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released Wednesday shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult. Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as […]
text:
People shop at an Ohio Walmart in April. Consumer spending driven by tax cuts and refunds, along with business investment in AI data centers, helped boost U.S. economic activity in the third quarter. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released Wednesday shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult.
Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as the artificial intelligence boom fueled investment while tax cuts and refunds kept shoppers going. The increase in gross domestic product could be a temporary bump, economists say.
“This level of GDP probably won’t be sustained in 2027. A slowdown in AI investment is likely, and many consumers don’t have much cushion left to handle higher prices,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a post on social media platform X.
The federal Bureau of Economic Analysis announced the revision Wednesday for inflation-adjusted GDP, a measure of economic activity. The third-quarter estimate was up significantly from an earlier estimate of 3.4%.
The 4.3% increase was the highest since 2023, when it was 4.5% in the third quarter.
The bureau said the increase was driven by gains in the value of computer software and consumer spending on pharmaceuticals, recreational goods and vehicles, while economic activity dropped in healthcare.
State estimates are not yet available for the third quarter. In the second quarter, when national growth was 2.2%, the largest annual growth was in New York (4.0%), followed by Delaware and South Carolina (both 3.5%). GDP decreased the most in West Virginia (down 2.3%), Wyoming (down 1.6%) and Alaska (down 1.3%), according to BEA statistics.
E.J. Antoni, a conservative economist once nominated to head the BEA, wrote in an X post that the “red-hot” increase makes a Federal Reserve interest rate hike “guaranteed.”
“Good news is bad news,” Antoni wrote.
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at [email protected].
This story was originally produced by Stateline, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Idaho Capital Sun, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

title: Boise State still projected for final College Football Playoff spot after San Diego State loss
summary: Even though Boise State has dropped out of the CFP Top 25, the selection committee’s current projections still leave the Broncos in position for the final playoff spot.
text:
BOISE, Idaho — For Boise State, the margin for error has always been small.
“We know the razor’s edge we live on at Boise State,” head coach Spencer Danielson said earlier this month. “You can’t have any hiccup.”
WATCH | Boise State still projected for final College Football Playoff
Last weekend, the Broncos had one.
Boise State’s home loss to San Diego State introduced new uncertainty into the Broncos’ College Football Playoff hopes after the team had been in position to claim the coveted final playoff berth reserved for the highest-ranked conference champion outside the Power Four.
Danielson said the Broncos aren’t focused on where they sit in the rankings right now.
“I don’t know, nor do I care where we get ranked right now in the college football pack,” Danielson said. “We lost on Saturday. That’s on us. We got to go play way better football on Saturday, and we got to find a way to play really good football two weeks from now in a championship game.”
READ MORE | Boise State drops to No. 22 in AP Top 25 poll after loss to San Diego State
The loss has already affected Boise State’s standing in the AP Poll. Liberty moved up to No. 21, while Boise State dropped to No. 22, marking the first time this season another non-Power Conference team has ranked ahead of the Broncos in that poll.
But the College Football Playoff rankings are the ones that ultimately matter.
Even though Boise State has dropped out of the CFP Top 25, the selection committee’s current projections still leave the Broncos in position for the final playoff spot.
“I believe our team is absolutely a team that belongs in the College Football Playoff,” Danielson said. “Absolutely. We got to keep getting better though.”
For Boise State, the path forward is straightforward: win.
The Broncos travel to face Colorado State this weekend in a Pac-12 flex game. Danielson acknowledged the challenge of winning away from home.
After Colorado State, Boise State returns home for a rematch against San Diego State in the Pac-12 Championship on Dec. 4.

title: Mitch Wieland Reads an Excerpt from his Novel, “The Ghosts of Okuma"
summary: On the fourth and final week of November, Mitch Wieland reads an excerpt from his new novel, “The Ghosts of Okuma.”
text:
“It felt to me like coming back to something from the past…or something that’s been lost, and trying to get it back, trying to reclaim it for your own,” our guest this month, Mitch Wieland said, about this month’s theme. “In my book, the two teenagers in the last act of the book, go back to their abandoned town near Fukushima to try to reclaim it…to try to make this empty town their own again.”
It’s the fourth and final week of November. We’re hearing writing along the theme of reclamation this month. Today, Mitch Wieland shares an excerpt from his new novel, “The Ghosts of Okuma,” recently named a Kirkus Editor’s Pick. Wieland is the author of Willy Slater’s Lane and God’s Dogs, a finalist for the John Gardner Fiction Book Award. Wieland is the founding editor of the Idaho Review and serves as the current Idaho Writer in Residence.
Something I Heard is supported by Idaho Commission on the Arts and the National Endowment for the Arts.

summary: This story was originally published by WyoFile on Nov. 25, 2026. For three summers during college, Barclay Trimble traveled from his native Texas to Yellowstone National Park, where he worked pumping gas at the Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge service stations. It represented his first meaningful encounter with America’s national park system. Trimble hiked and […]
text:
He once pumped gas at Yellowstone. Now he’s running the national park.
For Interim Superintendent Barclay Trimble, the new role ‘is like coming home.’
Interim Superintendent of Yellowstone National Park Barclay Trimble assumed his duties in October 2026. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)
This story was originally published by WyoFile on Nov. 25, 2026.
For three summers during college, Barclay Trimble traveled from his native Texas to Yellowstone National Park, where he worked pumping gas at the Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge service stations.
It represented his first meaningful encounter with America’s national park system. Trimble hiked and backpacked and explored on his time off hours and loved the experiences. And while today Trimble jokes that it’s “the one job that I never thought would show up on a resume,” he’s been reminded of that era during his first month in the role of Yellowstone’s acting superintendent.
Conservation groups, Forest Service add new public land near Yellowstone National Park
Trimble, a veteran National Park Service employee who has served in parks ranging from the Grand Canyon to Denali to Cape Hatteras National Seashore off the coast of North Carolina, filled the role that former superintendent Cam Sholly vacated in September.
At the helm of the country’s first national park, Trimble oversees 2.2 million acres of rugged landscapes, wildlife and geologic marvels that draw more than 4 million annual visitors — making it America’s third-most-visited park in 2025.
Since he started in October, Trimble has been working to get up to speed and understand the dynamics, issues and relationships that are critical for Yellowstone, he said.
“A lot of what I’m doing right now is still listening mode,” Trimble said. “I’m trying to learn from the park staff, I’m trying to learn from the state and federal partners, from the gateway communities and our tribal partners.”
And in the window of time he had before park sections began closing for the winter season, Trimble said, he got out to tour around, even visiting some of those old haunts from his gas station days.
“It’s good to come back and dust off the memory banks,” he said. “For me it really is kind of like coming home.”
    With decades of national park experience, Yellowstone’s interim superintendent settles in
Trimble brings a breadth of experience gained over 35 years in the agency. He served as acting superintendent of Grand Canyon National Park, worked in the Intermountain Region in Colorado and in Washington, D.C., and was the deputy regional director for the Southeast Region. Before coming to Yellowstone, he was the superintendent of Mammoth Cave National Park in Kentucky, which is home to the longest known cave system on Earth.
He’s happy to be back in the Mountain West, where he had spent about half of his career, he said.

title: Friday storm brings rain, wind and high-elevation snow to Idaho
summary: A mild Pacific storm will bring rounds of rain and mountain snow through Friday, followed by gusty winds and falling snow levels Friday night. Idaho ski areas see a mix of rain and high-elevation snow.
text:
A mild but moisture-rich Pacific storm will keep Thanksgiving weekend weather active across Idaho, bringing periods of valley rain, mountain snow and increasingly gusty winds through Friday night.
For holiday travelers, the biggest issue is the unusually high snow level. Snow levels will generally run between 6,500 and 8,500 feet through Friday, meaning many mountain roads and lower elevations will see rain rather than snow for much of the storm.
Above the snow line, 3 to 6 inches of snow is possible through Friday afternoon, with locally around 8 inches on favored west-facing slopes.
Friday night brings the biggest travel impacts
Weather conditions become more active Friday night as a cold front crosses the region.
Rain will become heavier for a time, winds will increase and snow levels will finally begin dropping. By Saturday morning, snow levels should range from roughly 5,000 to 8,000 feet, depending on location.
The heaviest snow will remain above about 6,500 feet, while elevations that remain entirely snow could receive 8 to 14 inches.
Travelers should also prepare for gusty winds Friday night. Gusts of 25 to 40 mph are expected across portions of southern Idaho, with gusts approaching 50 mph in some exposed areas.
Conditions improve Saturday as precipitation tapers off during the morning and most locations dry out during the afternoon.
Bogus Basin: Rain limits the new snow
The warm nature of this storm is working against Bogus Basin.
The resort reported a 21-inch base and 37 inches of season snowfall Thanksgiving Day, with 10 inches during the previous seven days. However, temperatures were above freezing and rain was falling Thursday afternoon. The resort's five-day forecast showed rain Friday and only 0 to 1 inch of snow Saturday. Bogus Basin Conditions & Webcams
That makes snow level the key factor. Much of Bogus sits in the elevation range where precipitation can switch between rain and snow during this storm.
The resort is already operating limited terrain, but early-season conditions remain. Bogus Basin also reported the road as snowpacked Thursday and recommended chains or snow tires.
Tamarack: A little snow now, better chance Monday
Tamarack Resort is also fighting the warmer pattern.
Tamarack reported 40 inches of total season snowfall at 7,700 feet, with a 16-inch summit base and 12-inch mid-mountain base Thursday. The resort remained closed with no lifts or runs operating.
Its forecast called for a mix of rain and snow Friday, with roughly 1 to 3 inches possible during the day and evening. The more promising period may arrive Monday, when Tamarack's resort forecast shows approximately 4 to 9 inches of potential snowfall.
The resort says the opening date remains a moving target because of incoming weather and snow conditions.
Brundage: Better positioned for natural snow
Brundage Mountain Resort could be one of the bigger winners because of its location farther north and its higher terrain.

title: US Supreme Court to weigh bans on AR-15s, similar guns in big Second Amendment case
summary: After a man used a semiautomatic rifle to kill five children and wound dozens of others at a California elementary school in 1989, officials in sprawling Cook County, Illinois, banned what they called assault weapons — certain firearms such as the AK-47 and AR-15. Decades later, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to decide whether […]
text:
US Supreme Court to weigh bans on AR-15s, similar guns in big Second Amendment case
SCOTUS will hold oral arguments Dec. 2 in potentially landmark gun rights case that could sweep away power of states, localities to prohibit popular models of firearms
The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
After a man used a semiautomatic rifle to kill five children and wound dozens of others at a California elementary school in 1989, officials in sprawling Cook County, Illinois, banned what they called assault weapons — certain firearms such as the AK-47 and AR-15.
Decades later, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to decide whether Cook County’s ban — and similar restrictions across the country — violate the Constitution.
The Supreme Court will hold oral arguments on Dec. 2 in a potentially landmark gun rights case that could sweep away the power of states and localities to prohibit popular models of firearms used in numerous mass shootings. The decision could also stop Congress from imposing new prohibitions on some semiautomatic weapons after a previous ban expired in 2004.
“The safety of our communities is at stake,” Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said in a statement. “There is absolutely no reason that AR-15s, AK-47s and other weapons of war that were designed to inflict mass carnage should be available to the public.”
States at odds
The case has pitted red and blue states against each other. Democratic state officials have urged the Supreme Court to uphold the bans, while Republicans say they must be invalidated under the Second Amendment.
Eleven states and the District of Columbia ban “assault weapons,” according to the advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety, which defines them as high-powered semiautomatic firearms. They include California, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington state.
Several major cities, such as Denver, Indianapolis, New York and Philadelphia, also have restrictions. Chicago is the county seat in Cook County.
The Supreme Court has spent nearly 20 years bolstering Americans’ rights to have guns and limiting the government’s power to restrict them. The justices first ruled in 2008 that the Second Amendment guarantees an individual right to bear arms for self-defense.
The court then said in 2022 that restrictions must be rooted in the country’s historical tradition of firearms regulation. The new standard spurred fresh challenges to modern-day laws limiting guns.
The justices will now decide whether bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic weapons — high-powered guns that fire and automatically reload each time the trigger is pulled — clear that high bar.

title: Temporary Protected Status to expire for Lebanese immigrants in the US
summary: WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May renewed TPS for an estimated 11,000 nationals from Lebanon for […]
text:
Temporary Protected Status to expire for Lebanese immigrants in the US
Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27
Markwayne Mullin, at the time a Republican senator from Oklahoma, speaks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. Mullin is now the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — Humanitarian protections for thousands of Lebanese immigrants living in the United States are set to expire by Nov. 27, and the Department of Homeland Security has not indicated if their Temporary Protected Status will be renewed.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in May renewed TPS for an estimated 11,000 nationals from Lebanon for six months, citing instability in the region due to the U.S.-Israel-backed war in Iran, which is still active.
Nationals who hail from a country deemed too dangerous for return, due to war, violence or other extreme instability, are granted anywhere from six-month to 18-month cycles of protections to remain and work in the U.S.
A DHS spokesperson did not answer State Newsroom’s questions about the renewal status for Lebanese immigrants with TPS.
“An announcement on Lebanon’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “Until such an announcement is made, Lebanese individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.”
DHS has made the same announcement for nationals with TPS from El Salvador, Sudan and Ukraine. TPS for people from all those countries expired this year, but DHS for now will allow those immigrants to also keep their work authorization and deportation protections.
Overall, the Trump administration has aimed to wind down the program created by Congress in the 1990s. At the start of the second Trump administration, 17 countries were designated under TPS, but now only Lebanon has the status, until Nov. 27.
The moves have resulted in more than 1 million immigrants having their TPS stripped, and opening them to the president’s mass deportation agenda.
The remaining TPS holders whose protections expired but who maintain deportation protections include roughly 200,000 Salvadorans, 100,000 Ukrainians and 2,000 Sudanese.
Congressional Democrats have tried to pass legislation to extend TPS broadly, and for certain nationals such as Haitians and Afghans, but have been unable to with Republicans controlling both chambers.
In January, Democrats will hold the majority in the House and Senate, and members of both chambers have expressed immigration reform as a top priority.
However, passage of any legal protections for immigrants will likely face a veto from President Donald Trump, and need a two-thirds majority to override.

title: Federal court blocks second Trump order on birthright citizenship
summary: WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group […]
text:
Federal court blocks second Trump order on birthright citizenship
Classwide injunction will remain in effect while litigation on case continues
Demonstrators from the immigration advocacy organization CASA chant “Up up with liberation, down down with deportation” outside of the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday, May 15, 2025, as justices heard oral arguments on the Trump administration’s legal challenge to birthright citizenship. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia Wednesday issued a classwide injunction to prevent the Trump administration from implementing its second attempt at redefining the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.
The order from Judge Christopher Reid Cooper will remain in effect while litigation continues. A classwide injunction blocks action affecting a defined group of individuals, as opposed to a nationwide injunction.
In a memorandum opinion, Cooper noted the Supreme Court earlier this year denied President Donald Trump’s executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born from immigrants either in the country unlawfully or on a temporary basis, in the case Barbara v. Trump.
“Yet Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued a second executive order—Executive Order 14418, at issue here—directing federal agencies to withhold recognition of citizenship from additional categories of U.S.-born children with noncitizen parents,” he wrote. “As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.”
The American Civil Liberties Union, which led the first challenge against the Trump administration’s birthright citizenship order and is leading the second, welcomed the ruling.
“Enough is enough,” Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.”
The Department of Justice did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.
Earlier this month, Cooper seemed skeptical of the legality of the Trump administration’s second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship.
The president’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.”
The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.

title: Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
summary: KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards. As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and […]
text:
Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones.
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations.
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program.

title: Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
summary: The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the […]
text:
Human rights groups sue ICE alleging detention of pregnant, nursing immigrants
Lawsuit cites 2021 ICE directive, which states agents shouldn’t ‘detain, arrest, or take into custody’ anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing
Federal immigration officers are shown at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in March. A lawsuit filed by advocacy organizations alleges the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is violating a 2021 directive by detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing women. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
The Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and several other groups filed a lawsuit Tuesday against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement alleging that the agency is illegally detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants against its own policies.
The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, cites a 2021 ICE directive, which states that agents “should not detain, arrest, or take into custody for an administrative violation” anyone who is known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing.
According to the complaint, ICE has stopped tracking the number of women who are pregnant, postpartum or nursing and being held in detention under the Trump administration. But one of the plaintiff organizations — the Women’s Refugee Commission — obtained data through a Freedom of Information Act request. Those documents showed an increase of pregnant women in ICE detention between January 2025 and March 2026 from nine to 128, or a 1,320% increase, the complaint states.
The length of detention for pregnant women has also increased substantially, according to the complaint.
“Since 2025, ICE detained more than 557 pregnant women for an average of 43 days,” the complaint reads. “Nearly 14% of these women were detained for 90 days or longer, with one woman detained for 219 days, almost seven months of her pregnancy.”
A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security said in an email sent to Stateline that the 2021 directive is still in place, and that pregnancy in ICE detention is “exceedingly rare,” making up 0.15% of all of those currently in custody as of Oct. 31.
The spokesperson said pregnant women in detention receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and other accommodations.
“This includes medical, dental, and mental health intake screening within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility, a full health assessment within 14 days of entering ICE custody or arrival at a facility, and access to necessary medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care,” the statement said. “This is the best healthcare many of these individuals have received in their entire lives.”

title: Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
summary: Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports. Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many […]
text:
Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise
Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns limit workforce
Turkeys gather for feeding at Whiffletree Farm in Virginia in September. Turkey production is up this year after two years of decline but prices rose because of strong demand and a shortage of whole birds. (Photo courtesy of Whiffletree Farm)
Turkey production for Thanksgiving has increased this year for the first time since avian diseases reduced supplies for years, but prices still rose as labor shortages created bottlenecks, according to federal reports.
Turkey farmers, like other livestock producers, say they need more foreign workers as immigration crackdowns and the ending of protected status for many immigrants take a toll on their workforce. Many producers support proposed bipartisan federal legislation to give them more access to visas for temporary workers.
Disruptions to Temporary Protected Status for some immigrants “could create significant operational challenges and further tighten an already constrained labor market,” Leslee Oden, CEO of the National Turkey Federation, wrote in an October op-ed supporting the federal visa legislation.
“This is a good first step to help packers and processors keep the rural economy moving and to ensure American consumers have access to affordable food,” Meat Institute CEO Julie Anna Potts said in a statement earlier this year.
Minnesota, North Carolina and Arkansas last year had the highest turkey production numbers, and millions of turkeys were also produced in Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Virginia, according to a U.S. Department of Agriculture report.
Wholesale prices shot up to a projected $1.76 a pound for whole hen turkeys this year from $1.36 last year and just 94 cents in 2024, according to the USDA, a 30% one-year increase. But a Farm Bureau report found retail prices for turkey up only about 10% from last year as retailers used turkey promotions to draw customers – some reported prices as low as 69 cents per pound.
Production increased this year to 5.1 billion pounds, after dropping two years in a row to as low as 4.8 billion pounds last year, but it’s still well below 2020’s 5.7 billion, according to the USDA report.
“They’ve had a lot of disease pressure over the years, so they’re still building up production numbers. That being said, grocery stores love to offer turkey deals,” said Farm Bureau Deputy Chief Economist Faith Parum in a November podcast.
Jesse Straight, who sells about 1,000 turkeys a year directly to customers at his Whiffletree Farm in Warrenton, Virginia, said he hasn’t been as affected by labor and disease issues as other, larger operations. His birds live outside on pastures with more fresh air than factory farms, and he pays a small staff fair wages, he said.
